cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus, is writing a letter to God's people in Rome (Romans 1:1, 7). He just finished a long list of what people do when they turn away from God: greed, envy, gossip, arrogance, the whole lineup (Romans 1:29-30). Now he turns to the one who passes judgment on another.

cards.question: Paul tells the person passing judgment on others that they have no excuse. What reason does he give?
Paul says God's judgment against those who do such things is based on truth.

cards.text: Then Paul asks the judge: you pass judgment on others and do the same things, and you think you'll escape God's judgment? Or are you ignoring the riches of His kindness, tolerance and patience?

cards.question: Paul says the judge doesn't realize where God's kindness leads. Where does it lead?

cards.text: But Paul says the judge has a hard and unrepentant heart. Because of it, he's piling something up against himself for later.

cards.question: Paul says that because of a hard and unrepentant heart, the judge is storing up ___ against himself for the day God's righteous judgment will be revealed.

cards.text: Then Paul says God "will repay each one according to his deeds." Each one, and nobody gets skipped.

cards.question: Some people keep at doing good, seeking glory, honor and immortality. What does Paul say God will give them?
Paul says there will be peace for those who are self-seeking, reject the truth and follow wickedness.

cards.text: Paul keeps going: there will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.

cards.question: For everyone who does good, Paul says glory, honor and peace come to the Jew but not to the Greek.
Evil brings trouble and good brings glory, for the Jew and for the Greek alike. What reason does Paul give?

answers.text: God gives the Jews more time

cards.text: Now Paul brings in the law. He says all who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law.

cards.question: And Paul says all who sin under the law will be ___ by the law.

cards.text: So being under the law doesn't get anyone out of being judged. Next, Paul says who will be declared righteous before God.

cards.question: Who does Paul say will be declared righteous before God?

cards.text: Then Paul talks about Gentiles, people who don't have the law. When they do by nature what the law requires, he says they are a law to themselves.

cards.question: When Gentiles do what the law requires without having the law, what does Paul say that shows?

answers.text: The law's work is written on their hearts
The law's words are written on their doorposts
The law's teaching came down from their elders

cards.question: Paul says their ___ also bear witness, with their thoughts either accusing or defending them.
Paul points to the day when God will judge men's secrets. Through whom will God judge them?

cards.text: Paul says that's what his gospel proclaims. Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I can tell you: there's no back of the drawer God can't see.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is almost missing. Stop 1 has no real laugh anywhere. Its only touches of personality are "the whole lineup" (card 1) and "nobody gets skipped" (card 8). Most story cards just restate the verse in plain words: stop 1 cards 4, 6 and 11, and stop 2 cards 1, 3 and 5. The one callback, in stop 2 card 9, is warm but not funny. Several moments could hold a clean laugh without muddying a fact: the judge doing the very thing he judges, storing up wrath, hearers versus doers.

rule.text: Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The person Paul addresses is called "the judge" in card 4, and the label carries into cards 5, 6 and 7. The text calls him "you who pass judgment" and "O man." "The judge" reads like an official title. It is also easy to confuse with God, who is the actual Judge in these verses.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "Jew" and "Greek" first appear here with no word on who they are. In this passage, "Greek" stands for non-Jews. A baker could take it to mean only people from Greece, and that would muddy cards 12 and 13 and the point that God does not show favoritism.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The first sentence ("So being under the law doesn't get anyone out of being judged") only restates the answer to card 2. It doesn't move the passage forward, so half the card is recap.
The question opens with "Paul says their ___ also bear witness" but never says who "their" is. The Gentiles were named on card 6, which is no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.
